source: The tendon spring operates optimally at relatively high strains as this increases the utilisation of elasticity (Lichtwark, 2005; Lichtwark and Wilson, 2006), but as a consequence, the risk of developing tendon injuries, such as chronic painful tendinopathy or acute tendon ruptures, increases (Magnan et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2018).

claim: A commercially available FEA software (ANSYS v19.0) was used for mesh generation and static stress analysis.
source: A commercially available FEA software (ANSYS v19.0, Ansys Inc, Canonsburg, PA) was used for mesh generation and static stress analysis.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis software.

claim: Each sub-tendon was modelled as a hyperelastic, non-linear, neo-Hookean material with the initial modulus obtained by curve-fitting the in vitro axial tensile testing results.
source: Each sub-tendon was modelled as a hyperelastic, non-linear, neo-Hookean material (Handsfield et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2017) with the initial modulus (Lat. G: 226.7 MPa, Med. G: 143.2 MPa, Soleus: 103.1 MPa) obtained by curve-fitting the in vitro axial tensile testing results.
evidence: This describes the material model used in FEA with citations.

claim: Sub-tendons were meshed into quadratic 10-node tetrahedral solid elements (TET10).
source: Sub-tendons were meshed into quadratic 10-node tetrahedral solid elements (TET10).
evidence: This describes the meshing procedure.

claim: A mesh convergence test was conducted using static stress analysis with criteria of 1% for each model.
source: A mesh convergence test was conducted using static stress analysis with criteria of 1% for each model.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedure for the FEA.

claim: Maximal element edge length for each model was 0.8, 0.5, and 0.4 mm, respectively, and yielded 258402, 195286, and 223423 elements, respectively.
source: Maximal element edge length for each model was 0.8, 0.5, and 0.4 mm, respectively, and yielded 258402, 195286, and 223423 elements, respectively.
evidence: This describes the mesh parameters.

claim: The contact faces between sub-tendon pairs were manually selected and assigned different contact properties: frictionless, frictional (with coefficient 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) and bonded.
source: The contact faces between sub-tendon pairs were manually selected and assigned different contact properties: frictionless, frictional (with coefficient 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) and bonded.
evidence: This describes the FEA setup.

claim: Surface-to-surface translational joints, with no restriction along the longitudinal axis while limiting transverse plane separation, were assigned at the contact faces to prevent sub-tendon separation.
source: Surface-to-surface translational joints, with no restriction along the longitudinal axis while limiting transverse plane separation, were assigned at the contact faces to prevent sub-tendon separation.
evidence: This describes the FEA setup.

claim: Fixed displacement at distal faces (to mimic the fixed calcaneus insertion) and individual 100 N linear ramped tensile forces at the proximal face of each sub-tendon (to mimic muscular pull) were applied.
source: Fixed displacement at distal faces (to mimic the fixed calcaneus insertion) and individual 100 N linear ramped tensile forces at the proximal face of each sub-tendon (to mimic muscular pull) were applied.
evidence: This describes the boundary conditions and loading in the FEA.

claim: Participants were assigned into two groups according to their age (Young: 20–30 years, n = 9; Old: over 50 years, n = 7).
source: Participants were assigned into two groups according to their age (Young: 20–30 years, n = 9; Old: over 50 years, n = 7).
evidence: This describes the participant groups in the in vivo study.

claim: The exclusion criteria were having any previous diagnosed Achilles tendon injuries and any systematic disease that may affect muscle-tendon functions.
source: The exclusion criteria were having any previous diagnosed Achilles tendon injuries and any systematic disease that may affect muscle-tendon functions.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the in vivo study.

claim: The participants were prone on an examination bed with feet firmly step against the wall (~90°).
source: The participants were prone on an examination bed with feet firmly step against the wall (~90°).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for the in vivo study.

claim: Three pairs of 50 mm diameter electrodes were placed on the motor points of the three muscles bellies.
source: Three pairs of 50 mm diameter electrodes were placed on the motor points of the three muscles bellies (Botter et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure with citations.

claim: The skin was cleaned with alcohol swaps and shaved if necessary to ensure minimal intensity for inducing muscular contraction and minimising discomfort.
source: The skin was cleaned with alcohol swaps and shaved if necessary to ensure minimal intensity for inducing muscular contraction and minimising discomfort.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Each muscle was stimulated using a commercially available transcutaneous electrical neuromuscular stimulation device with 30 Hz, 300 μs pulse train, and an on–off cycle of 8 s (4 s on and 4 s off) for 2 min to induce tetanic contractions.
source: Each muscle was stimulated using a commercially available transcutaneous electrical neuromuscular stimulation device with 30 Hz, 300 μs pulse train, and an on–off cycle of 8 s (4 s on and 4 s off) for 2 min to induce tetanic contractions.
evidence: This describes the stimulation parameters.

claim: Before the stimulation, an ultrasound probe was placed at the musculotendinous junction of the three muscles to ensure proper image quality.
source: Before the stimulation, an ultrasound probe (2–8 MHz, 9L-D, LOGIQ S8, GE Healthcare, Buckinghamshire, UK) was placed at the musculotendinous junction of the three muscles to ensure proper image quality.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: During the stimulation, the intensity increased gradually (to ~20 mA) until visible displacement of the stimulated muscle was recorded, while at the same time, no visible contraction of other muscles was observed, before moving the probe to the soleus musculotendinous junction to measure its displacement.
source: During the stimulation, the intensity increased gradually (to ~20 mA) until visible displacement of the stimulated muscle (e.g. medial gastrocnemius) was recorded, while at the same time, no visible contraction of other muscles (e.g. lateral gastrocnemius and soleus) was observed, before moving the probe to the soleus musculotendinous junction to measure its displacement (Figure 7).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: At least three consecutive contractions were recorded and stored for offline analyses.
source: At least three consecutive contractions were recorded and stored for offline analyses.
evidence: This describes the data collection procedure.

claim: Randomised sequence and ample rest between stimulations were used to reduce artefacts.
source: Randomised sequence and ample rest between stimulations were used to reduce artefacts.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure to minimize confounds.

claim: The analysis was performed in a semi-automatic way using an in-house MATLAB code, utilising the Computer Vision Toolbox add-on for tracking displacements and correcting movement artefacts.
source: The analysis was performed in a semi-automatic way using an in-house MATLAB code (R2019a, MathWorks, Natick, MA), utilising the Computer Vision Toolbox add-on for tracking displacements and correcting movement artefacts.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: The peak soleus musculotendinous junction displacement of each stimulation trial was tracked and normalised by its contracted muscular displacements.
source: The peak soleus musculotendinous junction displacement of each stimulation trial was tracked and normalised by its contracted muscular displacements (for gastrocnemii: musculotendinous junction, for soleus: one distal muscle fascicle–aponeurosis junction; Figure 7, left), assuming the muscular displacement affects only by stimulation intensity, while sub-tendon displacement affects by interface sliding capacity.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: The distal soleus muscle fascicle–aponeurosis junction was arbitrarily chosen as the reference point.
source: We arbitrarily chose the distal soleus muscle fascicle–aponeurosis junction as the reference point (Muramatsu et al., 2001) since no clear anatomical landmark lies within the soleus muscle.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method with a citation.

claim: Kruskal–Wallis H tests were used for comparing mechanical properties among sub-tendons, and Mann–Whitney U tests were used for post hoc analysis.
source: Kruskal–Wallis H tests were used for comparing mechanical properties among sub-tendons, and Mann–Whitney U tests were used for post hoc analysis.
evidence: This describes the statistical methods.

claim: In vivo soleus junction displacement between groups was compared using Mann–Whitney U tests.
source: In vivo soleus junction displacement between groups was compared using Mann–Whitney U tests.
evidence: This describes the statistical methods.

claim: Level of significance was set at 0.05, two tailed.
source: Level of significance was set at 0.05, two tailed.
evidence: This describes the statistical methods.

claim: A minimum of total 12 participants for the in vivo study was determined by a priori sample size estimation (d = 1.9, α = 0.05, β = 0.90) using G*Power 3.1.9.
source: A minimum of total 12 participants for the in vivo study was determined by a priori sample size estimation (d = 1.9, α = 0.05, β = 0.90) using G*Power 3.1.9 (Universität Düsseldorf).
evidence: This describes the sample size calculation.
